title: Close the Tabs: An End of Term Ritual for School Leaders
author: Rebecca Lowman
source: Language for Leadership on Substack, December 18, 2025
summary: Lowman opens on a paradox: we tell students to close their tabs and focus, yet we (the teachers and leaders) are running ten projects simultaneously with half-finished work everywhere. The piece is brief and pointed: attention and finishing are connected skills. The work of deep understanding, real change, and genuine mastery requires the cognitive coherence that multitasking destroys. Lowman notes that closing the tabs is a practical move that serves a larger principle. In a world of infinite inputs and infinite projects, finishing something matters as much as starting. The implication for schools: if we want students to finish work, to feel the satisfaction of mastery, to see a project through from start to finish, we have to model it. That means leaders close their tabs first. Teachers follow. Students notice.
points: Attention and finishing are connected skills; multitasking destroys the cognitive coherence that deep understanding and genuine mastery require.
In a world of infinite projects, finishing something matters as much as starting; closure matters for the satisfaction and coherence of learning.
If we want students to finish work and experience mastery, leaders and teachers have to close their tabs first; students notice and follow the example.
quotes: As the autumn term winds down and we head towards the Christmas break, school leaders often find themselves carrying far more than festive cheer into the holidays. We often carry open loops — the mental “tabs” that never seem to close.

It's strangely common: the people we line manage often get the least of our time. Urgent parent emails, safeguarding triage, assessment deadlines…these soak up the hours. Meanwhile, your competent, dependable team members quietly keep everything afloat.

Ah, the last-minute paperwork. The document you meant to submit. The file you intended to upload. The resource you promised to send “later today.” These are the things that wake us at 3am on Christmas Eve, demanding attention from the depths of our subconscious.” “You don't need to solve these before Christmas. But you do need to name them. Write each worry on a piece of paper, just the problem, not the solution. Allow it to live there instead of in your mind. Let the page hold it over Christmas so that your brain doesn't have to.
January can feel like a cold plunge if the first week back hasn't been thought about in advance.

At the end of a long term, patterns reveal themselves. Perhaps you've particularly noticed: rising stress, recurring disorganisation, a structural issue in your school, a creeping sense of overwhelm. So ask: What words, ideas or emotions do I want the New Year to hold?

It has been a long term. Students are tired. Behaviour dips. Emotions run high. And sometimes the things students say or do can sit heavy with us long after the moment has passed. But remember the mantra: They are the children. We are the adults.
Close the tabs you can. Write down the ones you can't, and walk into the holiday knowing you have earned every moment of rest.” Archived from Language for Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.
